Both statements are true, but the reason describes a **consequence** rather than the
ground of the assertion.
**Step 1 — test the assertion.** Thermal radiation - the radiation a hot body emits
simply by being hot - is indeed **electromagnetic** ✓ It occupies mainly the
**infrared** part of the spectrum, with wavelengths from about 700 nm to 1 mm, and a
body hot enough emits in the visible too, which is why iron glows red and then white.
**Step 2 — test the reason.** Electromagnetic waves are self-sustaining oscillations of
electric and magnetic fields and need **no material medium** ✓ Thermal radiation
therefore travels through vacuum - which is how the Sun's heat reaches the Earth across
150 million kilometres of empty space. The reason is **true**.
**Step 3 — ask whether the reason explains the assertion.** It does not ✓ Needing no
medium is a **property** that follows from being electromagnetic; it is not the evidence
that thermal radiation **is** electromagnetic. The logic runs the other way round.
**What would count as an explanation.** Thermal radiation obeys the laws of reflection
and refraction, travels at **3 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹**, can be polarised, shows interference, and
its spectrum follows **Planck's law** - all hallmarks of electromagnetic waves ✓ Those
facts establish the assertion; the absence of a medium merely agrees with it.
**Step 4 — match to the options.** Both true, reason not the correct explanation ✓
**The three modes of heat transfer, for contrast.**
**conduction** - needs a medium, by molecular collision
**convection** - needs a fluid medium, by bulk movement
**radiation** - needs **no** medium at all ✓
Only the third is electromagnetic, and that is what sets it apart.
**Where thermal radiation sits in the spectrum.** By Wien's law, λ_max = 2·9 x 10⁻³/T ✓
A body at 300 K peaks near **10 µm**, deep in the infrared; the Sun at 5800 K peaks near
**500 nm**, in the visible - the same physics across the whole range.
∴ B.

In **vacuum** every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed, whatever its colour.
**Step 1 — recall the value.** In free space
c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀)
= **2·998 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✓
and nothing in that expression refers to frequency or wavelength - μ₀ and ε₀ are
constants of the vacuum itself.
**Step 2 — conclude.** Red, violet and every other colour travel at exactly **c** ✓ so
all colours have the same velocity in vacuum.
**Why colours separate in glass but not in vacuum.** Inside a material the light
interacts with the atoms, and that interaction depends on frequency ✓ The refractive
index therefore varies with colour - **dispersion** - and violet, being bent most,
travels slowest. A vacuum has nothing to interact with, so there is no dispersion at all.
**The evidence from the sky.** A distant supernova flares in every colour at once, and
after travelling for millions of years across space the colours still arrive
**together**, within seconds of one another ✓ Had their speeds differed by even one part
in 10¹⁵, they would arrive years apart. This is one of the most precise tests in physics.
**What dispersion would look like if it existed in vacuum.** The disc of the Sun would
be fringed with colour at every eclipse, and distant stars would twinkle through a
rainbow sequence ✓ Neither is observed.
**The relation that still holds for each colour.** c = νλ ✓ Violet has a higher
frequency and shorter wavelength than red, and red the reverse - but the **product** is
the same for both, which is exactly the statement that their speeds are equal.
**Reading the distractors.** **Red** ✗ and **violet** ✗ each single out one colour, and
in **glass** the answer would indeed be red; the question's "in vacuum" is what makes
them wrong here ✓ Note the contrast with the companion question about glass, where the
colours genuinely differ.
∴ all colours have the same velocity.

Looking in from the **edge** means looking along a steeply slanting line, and apparent
depth depends on the angle of view.
**Step 1 — recall the normal result.** Viewed from directly overhead, a submerged object
appears raised, at an apparent depth
d_apparent = d_real/n ✓
with n = 4/3 for water, so it seems about three-quarters as deep.
**Step 2 — see what changes near the edge.** That simple formula holds only for
**near-normal** viewing ✓ For rays leaving the water at a large angle to the vertical -
which is how the near edge of the object is seen - the apparent depth is **smaller**
still, so those points appear nearer the surface.
**Step 3 — see why that distorts the shape.** Points at different distances from the
edge are viewed along **different** angles, so each is raised by a **different** amount ✓
A flat object is no longer imaged flat: it appears bent and foreshortened.
**Step 4 — note the second effect.** Because the whole object is raised and compressed,
the angle it subtends at the eye is **smaller** than the angle the same object would
subtend in air ✓ The object looks flattened as well as displaced - which is the
statement keyed here.
**The everyday version of this.** A straight stick held obliquely in water looks
**bent** at the surface, and the submerged part looks shorter ✓ Looked at straight down,
the same stick merely looks shallower, not bent - the distortion is entirely a
consequence of the oblique view.
**Why total internal reflection also matters.** Light inside the water meeting the
surface beyond the critical angle - about **48·8°** for water - cannot escape at all ✓
So points far from the edge, seen at very glancing angles, may simply not be visible
from that position.
**A note on the original.** This question comes from a set allowing **more than one**
correct answer, in which the statements about apparent depth near the edge and about
total internal reflection are also marked correct, for the reasons given above ✓ In the
single-answer form used here, the statement about the subtended angle is the one keyed.
**Reading the remaining distractor.** "**Water in a trough acts as a lens and
magnifies**" ✗ - a plane water surface has no curvature and so no focal length; it
displaces the image but does not magnify it ✓
∴ the angle subtended by the image of the object at the eye is smaller than the actual
angle subtended by the object in air.
